     2|
     3|# Cycles
     4|
     5|This page defines how many cycles a program costs. A program's cost is the sum
     6|of its instructions' costs, and `bin/minivm` reports it as `cycles`
     7|([Running](running.md#command-line)).
     8|
     9|## Base cost
    10|
    11|Every instruction costs 4, plus the cost given for it in the
    12|[cost table](#cost-table). `OUT` costs only the 4.
    13|
    14|A run is stopped with an error if it does too much work; see the
    15|[work limit](running.md#program-rules).
    16|
    17|## String bytes
    18|
    19|The string bytes of a value are the number of bytes in it if it is a STR, and
    20|0 otherwise (including `NULL`).
    21|
    22|An [element-wise instruction](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)
    23|costs, for each element of its result, a base amount plus string bytes:
    24|
    25|| Instructions | Base per element |
    26||---|---|
    27|| `DIV` `IDIV` `MOD` | 6 |
    28|| `TRUNC` `YEAR` `MONTH` `DAY` `DOW` `DATEADD` `DATEDIFF` | 2 |
    29|| every other element-wise instruction | 1 |
    30|
    31|| Instructions | String bytes per element |
    32||---|---|
    33|| comparisons: `EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `IS` | the bytes of the shorter operand |
    34|| `LEN` | the bytes of its operand |
    35|| `ISNULL` `NVL` `IF` `NULLIF` `NULLIFE` | nothing |
    36|| every other element-wise instruction | 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
    37|
    38|A literal operand counts at every element, like the value it stands for.
    39|
    40|## Comparisons
    41|
    42|`SORT` and `TOPK` compare rows on their sort keys
    43|([sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)). One comparison of two rows
    44|costs, for each key examined until one differs, 2 plus the bytes of the
    45|shorter string.
    46|
    47|For example, on a table `t` whose STR column `s` and INT column `n` hold the
    48|rows `('ab', 5)` and `('ab', 7)`, comparing the two rows on keys
    49|`s ASC NL, n ASC NL` costs 2 + 2 for the first key, which is equal, and 2 + 0
    50|for the second, which differs: 6 in all. Sorting the two rows takes that one
    51|comparison:
    52|
    53|```text
    54|LOAD s, t.s
    55|LOAD n, t.n
    56|SORT o, s ASC NL, n ASC NL
    57|OUT  o
    58|```
    59|
    60|costs (4 + 2) + (4 + 2) + (4 + 2 x 2 rows + 6) + 4 = 30 cycles.
    61|
    62|## Cost table
    63|
    64|Cycles beyond the base 4 of each instruction:
    65|
    66|| Instruction | Cycles |
    67||---|---|
    68|| [`ADD`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`SUB`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`MUL`](instructions/arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) [`NEG`](instructions/arithmetic.md#neg) [`WRAP`](instructions/arithmetic.md#wrap) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
    69|| [`DIV`](instructions/arithmetic.md#div) [`IDIV`](instructions/arithmetic.md#idiv) [`MOD`](instructions/arithmetic.md#mod) | 6 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
    70|| [`TRUNC`](instructions/arithmetic.md#trunc) | 2 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |
    71|| [`EQ`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`NE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`LT`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`LE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`GT`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is) | 1 per element, plus the bytes of the shorter operand |
    72|| [`AND`](instructions/logic.md#and-or) [`OR`](instructions/logic.md#and-or) [`NOT`](instructions/logic.md#not) | 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |

    75|| [`LEN`](instructions/strings.md#len) | 1 per element, plus the bytes of its operand |
    76|| [`YEAR`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`MONTH`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`DAY`](instructions/dates.md#year-month-day) [`DOW`](instructions/dates.md#dow) [`DATEADD`](instructions/dates.md#dateadd) [`DATEDIFF`](instructions/dates.md#datediff) | 2 per element, plus 1 per byte of each string operand (literals included) and of its result |

    79|| [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) | 2 per row, plus every [comparison](#comparisons) of a stable top-down merge sort |
    80|| [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#topk) | 2 per row, plus every [comparison](#comparisons) of a bounded insertion buffer (each row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search), plus 1 per buffered row shifted |
    81|| [`NLJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string key; plus 2 per output pair |
    82|| [`HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes; plus 2 per output pair |
    83|| [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) | per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys |
    84|| [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md#gall) [`GID`](instructions/grouping.md#gid) [`GFIRST`](instructions/grouping.md#gfirst) | 1 per row |
    85|| [`GCOUNT`](instructions/grouping.md#gcount) [`GCOUNTV`](instructions/grouping.md#gcountv) [`GSUM`](instructions/grouping.md#gsum) | 2 per row |
    86|| [`GMIN`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax) [`GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax) | 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string |
    87|| [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#out) | nothing |
    88|
    89|## Example
    90|
    91|On a table `t` whose STR column `s` holds `'ab'`, `'cde'`, `NULL`:
    92|
    93|```text
    94|LOAD  x, t.s
    95|UPPER u, x
    96|EQ    e, u, 'AB'
    97|OUT   e
    98|```
    99|
   100|| Instruction | Cost | Cycles |
   101||---|---|---|
   102|| `LOAD x, t.s` | 4 + 3 values | 7 |
   103|| `UPPER u, x` | 4 + (1 + 2 + 2) + (1 + 3 + 3) + (1 + 0 + 0) | 17 |
   104|| `EQ e, u, 'AB'` | 4 + (1 + 2) + (1 + 2) + (1 + 0) | 11 |
   105|| `OUT e` | 4 | 4 |
   106|| total | | 39 |
   107|
   108|`UPPER` pays for the bytes of its operand and of its result; `EQ` pays for the
   109|shorter of `u` and the literal `'AB'` at each row. `bin/minivm` prints
   110|`{"ncols":1,"rows":[[true],[false],[null]],"cycles":39}`.

1|# MiniVM
     2|
     3|MiniVM is a toy column virtual machine. It runs straight-line programs whose
     4|instructions each operate on whole columns of values, and it reports how many
     5|cycles each run costs.
     6|
     7|## Example
     8|
     9|```text
    10|LOAD    a, orders.o_amt
    11|GT      m, a, 100.00
    12|IDX     i, m
    13|GATHER  big, a, i
    14|OUT     big
    15|```
    16|
    17|- `LOAD` reads the stored column `orders.o_amt` into register `a`.
    18|- `GT` sets `m` to a BOOL column: `a > 100.00` at each row.
    19|- `IDX` sets `i` to the positions where `m` is TRUE.
    20|- `GATHER` sets `big` to the values of `a` at the positions in `i`.
    21|- `OUT` makes `big` the program's result.
    22|
    23|Saved as `big.mini`, run it from the bundle root:
    24|
    25|```sh
    26|bin/minivm big.mini examples/data.json
    27|```
    28|
    29|which prints `{"ncols": 1, "rows": [...], "cycles": C}` as one line of JSON; on
    30|`examples/data.json` that is 26 rows and 136 cycles. See [Running](running.md).
    31|
    32|## Contents
    33|
    34|- [Language](language.md): program syntax: lines, comments, opcodes, registers, operands, literals.
    35|- [Values](values.md): types, NULL, the NUM range, columns and group sets, ordering and comparison.
    36|- [Running](running.md): program rules and limits, errors, the command line, the table-set JSON format.
    37|- [Cycles](cycles.md): the cost model: base cost, string bytes, comparison cost, the full cost table.
    38|- [Instructions](instructions/README.md): conventions shared by all instructions, and an index of every opcode.
    39|  - [Arithmetic](instructions/arithmetic.md): `ADD` `SUB` `MUL` `DIV` `IDIV` `MOD` `NEG` `WRAP` `TRUNC`.
    40|  - [Logic](instructions/logic.md): `EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `IS` `AND` `OR` `NOT` `ISNULL` `NVL` `IF` `NULLIF` `NULLIFE`.
    41|  - [Strings](instructions/strings.md): `UPPER` `RTRIM` `TRIM` `LEFT` `SUBSTR` `LEN` `CAT`.
    42|  - [Dates](instructions/dates.md): `YEAR` `MONTH` `DAY` `DOW` `DATEADD` `DATEDIFF`.

     2|
     3|# Language
     4|
     5|This page gives the syntax of MiniVM programs: lines, comments, opcodes,
     6|registers, operands and literals.
     7|
     8|## Programs
     9|
    10|A program is straight-line: its instructions run once each, in order. Each
    11|line holds one instruction. A `;` starts a comment, which runs to the end of
    12|the line; a line may hold only a comment, or be blank. Spaces and tabs are
    13|interchangeable: they separate the opcode from its operands, and may indent a
    14|line or surround an operand.
    15|
    16|```text
    17|; Ids and amounts of orders over 100.
    18|load   id, orders.o_id
    19|load   amt, orders.o_amt
    20|gt     m, amt, 100      ; NULL where o_amt is NULL
    21|idx    i, m
    22|gather a, id, i
    23|gather b, amt, i
    24|out    a, b
    25|```
    26|
    27|The program must end with its only `OUT`; see [Program rules](running.md#program-rules).
    28|
    29|## Instructions
    30|
    31|An instruction is an opcode followed by comma-separated operands:
    32|
    33|```text
    34|OP dest, operand, ...
    35|```
    36|
    37|Opcodes are case-insensitive: `gt`, `Gt` and `GT` are the same instruction.
    38|So are the keywords `NULL`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `ASC`, `DESC`, `NF`, `NL` and
    39|`NULLEQ`.
    40|Each opcode's operands are given on its page in the
    41|[instruction reference](instructions/README.md).
    42|
    43|## Registers
    44|
    45|Register names are identifiers, such as `r1`, `amt` or `_t0`: a letter or `_`,
    46|followed by letters, digits and `_`. Register names are case-sensitive, and a
    47|keyword can't be a register name. A register holds a column or a group set
    48|([Values](values.md#columns-and-group-sets)) and can be overwritten.
    49|
    50|## Operands
    51|
    52|An operand is one of:
    53|
    54|| Operand | Example | Used by |
    55||---|---|---|
    56|| register | `amt` | every instruction |
    57|| literal | `100.00` | element-wise instructions, `FILL`, integer operands such as `LEFT`'s `n` |
    58|| `table.column` | `orders.o_amt` | [`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load) |
    59|| sort key | `amt DESC NL` | [`SORT`, `TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys) |
    60|| `NULLEQ` | `NULLEQ` | [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) |
    61|
    62|## Literals
    63|
    64|| Literal | Type | Notes |
    65||---|---|---|
    66|| `42`, `-7` | INT | must fit in 128 bits |
    67|| `12.50` | NUM | must be exact, in the [NUM range](values.md#num-range) |
    68|| `'it''s'` | STR | a quote inside the string is written twice |
    69|| `#2024-01-31#` | DATE | years 0001 to 9999 |
    70|| `NULL` | NULL | |
    71|| `TRUE`, `FALSE` | BOOL | |
    72|
    73|A literal stands for that value at every row.
    74|
    75|## Integer operands
    76|
    77|Some operands must be integer literals rather than registers: `n` and `len`
    78|(`LEFT`, `SUBSTR`, `SLICE`, `TOPK`) are non-negative, and `SUBSTR`'s `start` is
    79|at least 1. They may be arbitrarily large; a count larger than the input means
    80|all of it.

     3|# Values
     4|
     5|This page describes MiniVM's values and types, what a register holds, and how
     6|values are ordered and compared.
     7|
     8|## Types
     9|
    10|| Type | Values | Literal |
    11||---|---|---|
    12|| INT | exact 128-bit integer; a result outside -2^127 .. 2^127-1 is an error | `42` |
    13|| NUM | decimal: see [NUM range](#num-range) | `12.50` |
    14|| STR | string | `'it''s'` |
    15|| DATE | calendar date | `#2024-01-31#` |
    16|| BOOL | `FALSE` or `TRUE` | `TRUE` |
    17|
    18|`NULL` is a value of its own, written `NULL`. Unless an instruction says
    19|otherwise, an element-wise result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`
    20|([element-wise instructions](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)).
    21|
    22|Literal syntax is in [Literals](language.md#literals). Stored columns have
    23|type INT, NUM, STR or DATE ([table sets](running.md#table-sets)).
    24|
    25|## NUM range
    26|
    27|A NUM is below 1e28 in magnitude and has at most 28 digits after the point,
    28|and its digits without the point, read as an integer, are at most
    29|2^96 - 1 = 79228162514264337593543950335: 28 or 29 significant digits.
    30|A NUM keeps its digits after the point, so `1.0` and `1.00` are equal but
    31|print differently.
    32|
    33|A NUM literal or stored value must be such a number exactly; trailing zeros
    34|after the point are dropped as far as needed. A NUM result is rounded half to
    35|even to the most digits after the point that fit, and a result of magnitude
    36|1e28 or more is the error `numeric overflow`. Where an INT meets a NUM in
    37|arithmetic, and in `DIV`, an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude is that
    38|error too, even if the result would fit.
    39|
    40|## Columns and group sets
    41|
    42|A register holds either:
    43|
    44|- a **column**: a vector of values; or
    45|- a **group set**: a grouping of rows, made by
    46|  [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) or [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md#gall)
    47|  and read by the other [grouping instructions](instructions/grouping.md).
    48|
    49|Registers can be overwritten.
    50|
    51|## Ordering
    52|
    53|These instructions compare values:
    54|
    55|- [`EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) and [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is)
    56|- [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) and [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#topk)
    57|- the joins [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin)
    58|- [`GMIN`, `GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax)
    59|
    60|They order values as follows:
    61|
    62|| Values | Order |
    63||---|---|
    64|| INT and NUM | by numeric value, exactly at any magnitude; INT and NUM mix |
    65|| STR | by bytes |
    66|| DATE | by date |
    67|| BOOL | `FALSE < TRUE` |
    68|
    69|Comparing any other mix of types, such as STR with INT or DATE with NUM, is an
    70|error.
    71|
    72|String comparison is exact: there is no case folding, and trailing spaces
    73|count, so `'ab'` and `'ab '` differ, as do `'ab'` and `'AB'`.
    74|
    75|How each instruction treats `NULL` is given on its page; for sorts, see
    76|[sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys).
    77|

     3|# Running
     4|
     5|This page gives the rules every program must follow, what happens on an error,
     6|how to run a program with `bin/minivm`, and the JSON format of the tables it
     7|reads.
     8|
     9|## Program rules
    10|
    11|The last instruction must be the program's only [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#out).
    12|
    13|| Limit | Value |
    14||---|---|
    15|| instructions per program | at most 20,000 |
    16|| values held by one register | at most 4,000,000 (a join's output counts) |
    17|| values held by all registers together | at most 64,000,000; a long string counts as several values (about 1 per 32 bytes) |
    18|| work per run | roughly 300,000,000 [cycles](cycles.md); see below |
    19|| rows per table | at most 10,000 |
    20|| program file | at most 4 MiB |
    21|| table-set file | at most 32 MiB and 2,000,000 JSON values |
    22|
    23|The work limit stops runaway programs. It counts a run's cycles, but `HJOIN`
    24|and `GROUP` and copying long strings use it up faster than their cycles
    25|suggest, so such programs stop somewhat sooner. Exceeding it, like any other
    26|limit, is an error. It has no effect on the cycles reported for a run that
    27|finishes.
    28|
    29|## Errors
    30|
    31|Any error stops the program. No result is printed; the error goes to stderr
    32|and `bin/minivm` exits with status 1.
    33|
    34|## Command line
    35|
    36|```sh
    37|bin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json
    38|bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json
    39|```
    40|
    41|runs the program in `PROGRAM.mini` on the [table set](#table-sets) in
    42|`TABLES.json`. On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout and exits 0:
    43|
    44|```json
    45|{"ncols": N, "rows": [...], "cycles": C}
    46|```
    47|
    48|- `ncols` is the number of `OUT` operands.
    49|- `rows` is the result, one array of `ncols` values per row.
    50|  `NULL` is `null` and a BOOL is `true` or `false`. An INT is a JSON integer,
    51|  or a string of its digits outside -2^63 .. 2^63-1. A NUM is a string that keeps
    52|  its digits after the point (`"250.00"`), a STR a string, and a DATE a string
    53|  `"YYYY-MM-DD"`.
    54|- `cycles` is the program's cost ([Cycles](cycles.md)).
    55|
    56|| Exit status | Meaning |
    57||---|---|
    58|| 0 | success; the result is on stdout |
    59|| 1 | error; the message is on stderr |
    60|| 2 | wrong number of arguments; a usage line is on stderr |
    61|
    62|With the program from [Language](language.md#programs) saved as
    63|`over100.mini` and the [example table set](#example) as `orders.json`:
    64|
    65|```sh
    66|$ bin/minivm over100.mini orders.json
    67|{"ncols":2,"rows":[[1,"250.00"]],"cycles":42}
    68|```
    69|
    70|`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` prints the table set's [schema file](#schema-files)
    71|as one line of JSON instead of running a program.
    72|
    73|A program that compares a DATE with an INT stops with an error:
    74|
    75|```text
    76|LOAD d, orders.o_date
    77|GT   m, d, 5
    78|OUT  m
    79|```
    80|
    81|```sh
    82|$ bin/minivm bad.mini orders.json
    83|error: line 2: GT: expected a number, got DATE
    84|```
    85|
    86|## Table sets
    87|
    88|A table set is a JSON object mapping each table name to its columns and rows:
    89|
    90|```json
    91|{"<table>": {"columns": [{"name": "c", "type": "INT|NUM|STR|DATE"}], "rows": [[...], ...]}}
    92|```
    93|
    94|- Table and column names are identifiers (letters, digits and `_`, not starting
    95|  with a digit), compared without regard to case. Duplicate names are an error.
    96|- `columns` lists each column's `name` and `type`, one of `INT`, `NUM`, `STR`, `DATE`.
    97|- `rows` lists each row as an array of values, one per column, in column order.
    98|  A table without `rows` is empty.
    99|- A table may also declare [constraints](#constraints).
   100|- Any key other than those shown or listed there is an error, as is a repeated key.
   101|- A table holds at most 10,000 rows.
   102|- INT values are JSON integers that fit in 32 bits.
   103|- NUM values may be JSON numbers or strings. They must be exact, in the
   104|  [NUM range](values.md#num-range).
   105|- Dates are strings `"YYYY-MM-DD"`, years 0001 to 9999.
   106|- JSON `null` is `NULL`.
   107|
   108|A program reads a stored column with `LOAD d, table.column` ([`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load)).
   109|
   110|### Constraints
   111|
   112|A table may declare what its rows guarantee. `bin/minivm` checks every declared
   113|constraint when it reads the table set, and a table set that breaks one is an error.
   114|
   115|| Key | Example | Guarantee |
   116||---|---|---|
   117|| `key` | `["l_order", "l_no"]` | the columns are never `NULL`, and no two rows agree on all of them |
   118|| `not_null` | `["p_price"]` | the columns are never `NULL` |
   119|| `refs` | `{"l_prod": "products.p_id"}` | every non-NULL value of the column is a value of the other column, which must be its table's whole `key` and have the same type (INT and NUM may refer to each other) |
   120|| `check` | `{"l_qty": [1, 500]}` | every non-NULL value lies between the bounds, inclusive; `null` leaves a side open; INT, NUM and DATE columns only |
   121|| `sorted` | `["l_order", "l_no"]` | the rows are stored in ascending order of the columns, as `ASC NF` sorts them |
   122|
   123|Values are compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering), so NUM keys `1.0` and
   124|`1.00` are the same key. Column names in constraints are compared without regard
   125|to case, and naming a column twice in one constraint is an error. A table may refer to itself.
   126|
   127|```json
   128|{
   129|  "orders": {"columns": [{"name": "o_id", "type": "INT"}], "key": ["o_id"], "rows": [[1], [2]]},
   130|  "lines": {
   131|    "columns": [{"name": "l_order", "type": "INT"}, {"name": "l_qty", "type": "INT"}],
   132|    "refs": {"l_order": "orders.o_id"}, "check": {"l_qty": [1, null]}, "sorted": ["l_order"],
   133|    "rows": [[1, 3], [1, 1], [2, 5]]
   134|  }
   135|}
   136|```
   137|
   138|### Example
   139|
   140|```json
   141|{
   142|  "orders": {
   143|    "columns": [
   144|      {"name": "o_id",     "type": "INT"},
   145|      {"name": "o_amt",    "type": "NUM"},
   146|      {"name": "o_date",   "type": "DATE"},
   147|      {"name": "o_status", "type": "STR"}
   148|    ],
   149|    "rows": [
   150|      [1, 250.00,   "2024-01-31", "shipped"],
   151|      [2, "99.5",   "2024-02-01", ""],
   152|      [3, null,     "2024-02-03", null]
   153|    ]
   154|  }
   155|}
   156|```
   157|
   158|## Schema files
   159|
   160|`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` describes a table set without its rows: each table's
   161|columns and [constraints](#constraints), as in the table set, plus a `stats` object
   162|summarizing its rows:
   163|
   164|```json
   165|{"<table>": {"columns": [...], "key": [...], ..., "stats": {"rows": N, "columns": {"<column>": {"nulls": N, "distinct": N, "min": v, "max": v, "common": [[v, N], ...], ...}}}}}
   166|```
   167|
   168|The constraints hold for every table set with this schema; the stats describe only this one.
   169|
   170|| Stats field | Meaning |
   171||---|---|
   172|| `rows` | rows in the table |
   173|| `nulls` | `NULL` values in the column |
   174|| `distinct` | distinct non-NULL values, compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering) |
   175|| `min`, `max` | least and greatest non-NULL value; `null` if there is none |
   176|| `avg_bytes` | STR only: mean bytes of the non-NULL values, rounded to 2 decimal places; 0 if there are none |
   177|| `common` | up to 8 values that occur more than once, most frequent first (ties in value order), with their counts |
   178|| `histogram` | INT, NUM and DATE only, if any value is non-NULL: 11 bounds of 10 equal-count buckets of the sorted non-NULL values, from `min` to `max` |
   179|

     3|# Strings
     4|
     5|Element-wise operations on STR values. All instructions on this page follow the [element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions): the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`. Lengths and positions count characters; string-byte costs count bytes ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
     6|
     7|| Instruction | Result |
     8||---|---|
     9|| [`UPPER d, s`](#upper) | upper case (Unicode) |
    10|| [`RTRIM d, s`](#rtrim-trim) / [`TRIM d, s`](#rtrim-trim) | without trailing / leading and trailing spaces |
    11|| [`LEFT d, s, n`](#left) | first `n` characters |
    12|| [`SUBSTR d, s, start, len`](#substr) | `len` characters from 1-based `start` |
    13|| [`LEN d, s`](#len) | number of characters |
    14|| [`CAT d, a, b`](#cat) | concatenation |
    15|
    16|## `UPPER`
    17|
    18|```text
    19|UPPER d, s
    20|```
    21|
    22|`s` in upper case, by Unicode's full case mapping, which can change the number of characters: `UPPER('straße')` is `'STRASSE'`.
    23|
    24|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
    25|
    26|## `RTRIM`, `TRIM`
    27|
    28|```text
    29|RTRIM d, s
    30|TRIM  d, s
    31|```
    32|
    33|`s` without trailing spaces (`RTRIM`), or without leading and trailing spaces (`TRIM`). Only `' '` counts as a space.
    34|
    35|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
    36|
    37|## `LEFT`
    38|
    39|```text
    40|LEFT d, s, n
    41|```
    42|
    43|The first `n` characters of `s` (all of `s` if it is shorter). `n` is a non-negative [integer literal](../language.md#integer-operands).
    44|
    45|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
    46|
    47|## `SUBSTR`
    48|
    49|```text
    50|SUBSTR d, s, start, len
    51|```
    52|
    53|`len` characters of `s`, starting at the 1-based position `start` (fewer if `s` ends first). `start` (at least 1) and `len` are [integer literals](../language.md#integer-operands).
    54|
    55|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
    56|
    57|## `LEN`
    58|
    59|```text
    60|LEN d, s
    61|```
    62|
    63|INT: the number of characters in `s`.
    64|
    65|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
    66|
    67|## `CAT`
    68|
    69|```text
    70|CAT d, a, b
    71|```
    72|
    73|The concatenation of `a` and `b`.
    74|
    75|**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `a`, of `b` (literals included) and of the result ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
    76|
    77|## Example
    78|
    79|Given a table `t` whose STR column `s` holds `' ab '`, `''` and `'Zoë'`:
    80|
    81|```text
    82|LOAD  s, t.s
    83|TRIM  u, s
    84|CAT   c, u, '!'
    85|LEN   l, c
    86|OUT   c, l
    87|```
    88|
    89|prints `{"ncols":2,"rows":[["ab!",3],["!",1],["Zoë!",4]],"cycles":73}`. `'Zoë!'` has 4 characters but 5 bytes: `CAT` costs 1 + 4 + 1 + 5 = 11 cycles on that row, and `LEN` costs 1 + 5.

     3|# Instructions
     4|
     5|This page states the conventions shared by all instructions and indexes every opcode. Cycle costs are summarized in [Cycles](../cycles.md).
     6|
     7|## Notation
     8|
     9|Each instruction is shown as `OP` followed by its operands:
    10|
    11|- `d` is the destination register (`li`, `ri` for joins, `g` for group sets).
    12|- `a`, `b`, `c`, `s`, `x`, `y` are source operands: `c` is a condition, `s` usually a string or source column, `x` and `y` dates.
    13|- `n`, `start` and `len` are integer literals; `lit` is a literal.
    14|- `i` is a column of positions, `g` a group set, `key` a [sort key](sorting.md#sort-keys), `table.column` a stored column.
    15|
    16|Where an element-wise instruction takes a register operand, a literal may be used instead; it stands for that value at every row ([literals](../language.md#literals)).
    17|
    18|Positions are 0-based INT values.
    19|
    20|An operand that expects a column can't name a group set, and the reverse; either
    21|is an error, as is reading a register that hasn't been set.
    22|
    23|## Element-wise instructions
    24|
    25|The instructions on the [arithmetic](arithmetic.md), [logic](logic.md), [strings](strings.md) and [dates](dates.md) pages compute one result value per row:
    26|
    27|- All register operands must have the same length, which is the result's length.
    28|- At least one operand must be a register.
    29|- Unless noted, the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`. That comes first: `DIV` of NULL by 0 is NULL, not division by zero, and `ADD` of NULL and a STR is NULL, not a type error.
    30|- Types are checked row by row: an operand of the wrong type is an error only at a row where the instruction uses it, so whether a program fails can depend on its data. An empty column, or one of NULLs, never gives a type error.
    31|
    32|Given a table `t` whose INT column `x` holds `1`, `NULL`, `3`:
    33|
    34|```text
    35|LOAD  x, t.x
    36|ADD   y, x, 10      ; the literal 10 stands for 10 at every row
    37|OUT   y
    38|```
    39|
    40|prints `{"ncols":1,"rows":[[11],[null],[13]],"cycles":18}`.

     3|# Grouping instructions
     4|
     5|`GROUP` and `GALL` divide rows into groups and store them as a group set; the other instructions on this page read a group set and return columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).
     6|
     7|| Instruction | Result |
     8||---|---|
     9|| [`GROUP g, k, ...`](#group) | group set: rows with equal keys share a group |
    10|| [`GALL g, s`](#gall) | group set: one group holding every row of `s` |
    11|| [`GID d, g`](#gid) | group number of each row |
    12|| [`GFIRST d, g`](#gfirst) | position of each group's first row |
    13|| [`GCOUNT d, g`](#gcount) | rows per group |
    14|| [`GCOUNTV d, g, s`](#gcountv) | non-NULL values of `s` per group |
    15|| [`GSUM d, g, s`](#gsum) | sum of non-NULL values per group |
    16|| [`GMIN d, g, s` / `GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) | least / greatest non-NULL value per group |
    17|
    18|## Group sets
    19|
    20|A register holds either a column or a group set ([values](../values.md#columns-and-group-sets)). A group set assigns each of its rows a group number; groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance. [`GROUP`](#group) and [`GALL`](#gall) produce a group set. [`GID`](#gid) returns a column with one value per row; the aggregates [`GFIRST`](#gfirst) through [`GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) return a column with one value per group, the value for group `k` at position `k`. The `s` operand of an aggregate is a column over the same rows as the group set; a different length is an error.
    21|
    22|Aggregate columns of the same group set line up with each other. To label each group with its key, gather the key at [`GFIRST`](#gfirst). Orders per status:
    23|
    24|```text
    25|LOAD   st, orders.o_status
    26|GROUP  g, st
    27|GFIRST f, g
    28|GATHER key, st, f
    29|GCOUNT n, g
    30|OUT    key, n
    31|```
    32|
    33|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["open",7],["closed",12],["shipped",11]]`.
    34|
    35|## `GROUP`
    36|
    37|```text
    38|GROUP g, k, ...
    39|```
    40|
    41|Sets `g` to a group set over the rows of the key columns `k, ...`: rows with equal keys share a group, and NULL equals NULL. All key columns must have the same length. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): INT and NUM mix (`1` and `1.00` share a group), and a key column holding values that can't be compared (e.g. STR and INT) is an error.
    42|
    43|**Cycles:** per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
    44|
    45|## `GALL`
    46|
    47|```text
    48|GALL g, s
    49|```
    50|
    51|Sets `g` to a group set with one group holding every row of `s`, even when `s` is empty.
    52|
    53|**Cycles:** 1 per row.
    54|
    55|## `GID`
    56|
    57|```text
    58|GID d, g
    59|```
    60|
    61|Sets `d` to the group number of each row of `g`.
    62|
    63|**Cycles:** 1 per row.
    64|
    65|## `GFIRST`
    66|
    67|```text
    68|GFIRST d, g
    69|```
    70|
    71|Sets `d` to the position of each group's first row. The result is NULL for the group of an empty `GALL`.
    72|
    73|**Cycles:** 1 per row.
    74|
    75|## `GCOUNT`
    76|
    77|```text
    78|GCOUNT d, g
    79|```
    80|
    81|Sets `d` to the number of rows in each group.
    82|
    83|**Cycles:** 2 per row.
    84|
    85|## `GCOUNTV`
    86|
    87|```text
    88|GCOUNTV d, g, s
    89|```
    90|
    91|Sets `d` to the number of non-NULL values of `s` in each group.
    92|
    93|**Cycles:** 2 per row.
    94|
    95|## `GSUM`
    96|
    97|```text
    98|GSUM d, g, s
    99|```
   100|
   101|Sets `d` to the sum of the non-NULL values of `s` in each group: INT when all are INT, else NUM. The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values. A NUM sum is computed exactly, with as many digits after the point as the value with the most, and rounded once as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range), so it doesn't depend on the order of the rows. Only each group's total is checked: a total outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, whatever the running sums along the way.
   102|
   103|**Cycles:** 2 per row.
   104|
   105|## `GMIN`, `GMAX`
   106|
   107|```text
   108|GMIN d, g, s
   109|GMAX d, g, s
   110|```
   111|
   112|Sets `d` to the least (`GMIN`) or greatest (`GMAX`) non-NULL value of `s` in each group, the first of equals: of `1`, `1.0` and `1.00`, whichever comes first. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering). The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values.
   113|
   114|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).
   115|

     2|
     3|# Join instructions
     4|
     5|`NLJOIN` and `HJOIN` pair up the rows of two key columns whose keys are equal and return the pairs as two position columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).
     6|
     7|| Instruction | Result |
     8||---|---|
     9|| [`NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | positions of all pairs with `lk[i] = rk[j]` |
    10|| [`HJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | same result as `NLJOIN` |
    11|
    12|## `NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`
    13|
    14|```text
    15|NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
    16|HJOIN  li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
    17|```
    18|
    19|Finds all pairs `(i, j)` with `lk[i] = rk[j]`, ordered by `i` then `j`. Sets `li` to the positions into `lk` and `ri` to the positions into `rk`, one entry per pair; if `li` and `ri` are the same register, it holds the positions into `rk`. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): a non-NULL left key that can't be compared with a non-NULL right key (e.g. STR with INT) is an error. A NULL key matches no key, unless the optional `NULLEQ` flag is given, in which case NULL keys match each other. `HJOIN` gives the same result as `NLJOIN`, errors included; only the cost differs.
    20|
    21|**Cycles (`NLJOIN`):** per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string key ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.
    22|
    23|**Cycles (`HJOIN`):** per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.
    24|
    25|### Example
    26|
    27|[`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) through `li` picks columns of the left rows and through `ri` columns of the right rows, giving one row per pair. Customers with their region's name:
    28|
    29|```text
    30|LOAD   reg, customers.c_region
    31|LOAD   code, regions.r_code
    32|HJOIN  li, ri, reg, code
    33|LOAD   cname, customers.c_name
    34|LOAD   rname, regions.r_name
    35|GATHER c, cname, li
    36|GATHER r, rname, ri
    37|OUT    c, r
    38|```
    39|
    40|On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["Cy","Southern"],["Dee","West Coast"],["Eve","Southern"], ...]`.
    41|

     4|
     5|Element-wise comparisons, BOOL logic and NULL handling. All instructions on this page follow the [element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions); where an instruction's NULL behavior differs from the default (the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`), its section says so.
     6|
     7|| Instruction | Result |
     8||---|---|
     9|| [`EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `d, a, b`](#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | BOOL comparison |
    10|| [`IS d, a, b`](#is) | BOOL, never NULL: equal, or both NULL |
    11|| [`AND d, a, b`](#and-or) / `OR` | three-valued logic |
    12|| [`NOT d, a`](#not) | BOOL negation |
    13|| [`ISNULL d, a`](#isnull) | BOOL, never NULL |
    14|| [`NVL d, a, b`](#nvl) | `a`, or `b` when `a` is NULL |
    15|| [`IF d, c, a, b`](#if) | `a` where `c` is TRUE, else `b` |

    19|## `EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`
    20|
    21|```text
    22|EQ d, a, b
    23|NE d, a, b
    24|LT d, a, b
    25|LE d, a, b
    26|GT d, a, b
    27|GE d, a, b

    29|

    35|
    36|```text
    37|IS d, a, b
    38|```

    45|
    46|```text
    47|AND d, a, b
    48|OR  d, a, b

    53|| `a` | `b` | `AND` | `OR` |
    54||---|---|---|---|
    55|| `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` |
    56|| `TRUE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` |
    57|| `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` |
    58|| `TRUE` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `TRUE` |
    59|| `FALSE` | `NULL` | `FALSE` | `NULL` |
    60|| `NULL` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `NULL` |

    69|NOT d, a

    77|

    86|## `NVL`

    88|```text
    89|NVL d, a, b

    97|

    99|IF d, c, a, b

   109|NULLIF d, a, b

     3|# Sorting instructions
     4|
     5|`SORT` and `TOPK` order the rows of one or more key columns and return positions, which [`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) applies to any column of the same rows. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).
     6|
     7|| Instruction | Result |
     8||---|---|
     9|| [`SORT d, key, ...`](#sort) | positions of the rows in stable sorted order |
    10|| [`TOPK d, n, key, ...`](#topk) | the first `n` positions of the same order |
    11|
    12|## `SORT`
    13|
    14|```text
    15|SORT d, key, ...
    16|```
    17|
    18|Sets `d` to the positions of the rows in stable sorted order by the [sort keys](#sort-keys).
    19|
    20|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a stable top-down merge sort ([comparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)).
    21|
    22|## `TOPK`
    23|
    24|```text
    25|TOPK d, n, key, ...
    26|```
    27|
    28|Sets `d` to the first `n` positions of the order `SORT` would produce for the same keys (all of them if there are fewer rows). `n` is an integer literal.
    29|
    30|**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a bounded insertion buffer (each row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search) ([comparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)), plus 1 per buffered row shifted.
    31|
    32|## Sort keys
    33|
    34|```text
    35|reg ASC|DESC NF|NL
    36|```
    37|
    38|A sort key is a register followed by a direction and a NULL placement, separated by spaces or tabs; all three parts are required. All key columns must have the same length. Rows are ordered by the first key, then by each following key among rows the earlier keys leave equal.
    39|
    40|- `ASC` orders values from least to greatest, `DESC` reverses the order of values. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering).
    41|- `NF` puts NULLs first and `NL` puts them last, whatever the direction.
    42|- Ties keep their input order.
    43|
    44|Customers by credit, highest first with NULLs last, then by name:
    45|
    46|```text
    47|LOAD   name, customers.c_name
    48|LOAD   credit, customers.c_credit
    49|SORT   p, credit DESC NL, name ASC NF
    50|GATHER n, name, p
    51|GATHER c, credit, p
    52|OUT    n, c
    53|```

Starting with q0007, the simplest program: it loads seven order columns, then applies nvl, concatenation, nullif, left, upper, and day-of-week computations. I need to trace which results actually feed into the output versus which are dead code, like the upper() result and the DOW computation that may or may not matter depending on error behavior.

Since o_date is a proper DATE column, DOW on NULL just returns NULL rather than erroring, so that computation is dead and safe to remove. Similarly upper() on the note string can't error, so dropping dead code here won't introduce new failures.

Then the program sorts all 30 rows by amount descending (nulls last) and id ascending, gathers everything, filters to year 2023 month 7, and takes the top 5, outputting id, amount, and the concatenated/truncated string. Since id is unique and non-null, the sort is total, so filtering before or after the top-5 slice should be equivalent — and the year/month filter can be rewritten as a date range check between July 1 and July 31, 2023, with NULL dates naturally excluded.

I'm now comparing instruction costs between the year+month equality approach versus a GE/LE range check with AND, trying to find the cheapest way to express the July 2023 filter given the 30-row dataset, since a single-comparison trick like DATEDIFF doesn't avoid needing two bounds.
